round_scores.evidence: Turn 1 — Agent D: "...I get home and the stove is busy. By the time it's free, it's after nine. When am I supposed to cook?" (A direct, substantive complaint about access to the stove.)

Turn 3 — Agent B: "The smell gets in my room. I have to be up for work at five." Turn 4 — Agent C: "...Maybe we should actually agree on how we're going to use it." (Multiple substantive problems now present: smells, scheduling, shared rules.)

Turn 5 — Agent D: "I agree. A schedule or something would be good. Then I'd know when I can get to the stove." Turn 6 — Agent C: "A schedule for the stove is a start. We also need to agree on cleaning." (Proposals introduced but no settlement; clear disagreements persist about multiple issues.)

Turn 7 — Agent D: "...can we settle the stove schedule first? That's the most urgent thing for me right now." Turn 8 — Agent A: "Why just the stove? What about the pan? Or the incense? If we're making rules, we make rules for everything." (Explicit incompatibility over agenda/priorities.)

Turn 9 — Agent B: "For the smell, can we just agree to close the kitchen door and use the fan?" Turn 10 — Agent A: "Okay, fine. Door and fan." (Mutual, concrete agreement on the smell issue reduces one substantive conflict, while stove/cleaning/incense remain unresolved.)

Turn 11 — Agent B: "Okay, thanks. That's all I needed." Turn 12 — Agent A: "...So what about the rest of it? The pan is still there. The stove is still an issue." (Smell remains settled; other substantive issues persist with no progress.)

Turn 13 — Agent B: "Like I said, that's all I needed. The rest is up to you all." Turn 14 — Agent C: "See? This is why we need to agree on everything together. ... We can't just solve one person's problem and then leave." (Conflict over participation and responsibility intensifies.)

Turn 15 — Agent D: "Okay, you're right. Let's sort it all out together. As long as a stove schedule is part of it." Turn 16 — Agent C: "Good. So, stove schedule, and cleaning. How about we start with a simple rule: if you use the kitchen, you clean up after yourself right away." (Group moves toward joint problem-solving and a concrete cleaning rule is proposed, but not yet accepted by every party.)

substantive_insights: There are multiple overlapping practical problems (access to stove, odors affecting sleep/work, and shared cleaning) that require different remedies.
Agents have different priorities: D prioritizes predictable stove access; B prioritizes eliminating smells for sleep; C prioritizes shared cleaning norms.
Partial, single-issue agreements (the door+fan) can settle one party's urgent need but leave collective-action problems unresolved.
One participant's withdrawal (B) after their issue is solved reduces momentum for solving the remaining shared problems.
